2612.heavy: 'The term heavy vowel denotes a potentially stressed vowel, i.e. a) a full single vowel, and b) a head vowel' (p. 39), a head vowel being the first vowel of a vowel sequence. Light = the 'empty vowel' /ə/ (never stressed, never word-initial or word-final), plus, in Koci and rarely in Kotgarhi, a single non-final unstressed /i/ or /u/ treated as empty. Vowel length /: and consonant length are not the criterion: 'Consonant quantity (long and short) and stress have a low phonemic status, long quantity being, with a few exceptions, connected with certain consonants... the stress being connected with certain vowel features' (p. 12). Diachronically (p. 67) the stressed vowel continues 'the last non-final long vowel' of the Middle-Indian form, 'b) in other cases, the first vowel of the word'.
2612.dflt: Not applicable by the source's definitions: every non-clitic word contains at least one heavy vowel ('Each word which is not enclitic or proclitic has one stress-syllable'; 'If there is only one heavy vowel it of course bears the stress'), /ə/ never occurring word-initially or word-finally.
2612.prule: Every non-clitic word has exactly one stress syllable, on the first (leftmost) 'heavy' vowel, where heavy = a full (non-reduced) vowel that stands alone between consonants or heads a vowel sequence; the reduced 'empty' vowel /ə/ is never stressed. A word has at most two heavy vowels; when there are two, the first is stressed and the second is word-final and unstressed. Final morphemes are never stressed. Stress is thus a function of vowel quality (full vs. reduced), not of syllable count, and surfaces on the 1st, 2nd or (rarely) 3rd syllable.
2612.srule: None in simplex words: 'Each word which is not enclitic or proclitic has one stress-syllable' (p. 39; e.g. five-syllable /neutieo/ with every vowel but the stressed head vowel unstressed, p. 43). Two stresses occur only in compound substantives, one per member ('Each member is stressed separately', p. 41; 'double stress', p. 109).

2614.prule: No word-stress rule: Mahou is a two-level (H/L) tone language with the syllable as TBU and tone melodies lexically specified per morpheme; the only 'stress' recognised is a lexically listed, binary, whole-morpheme feature ('morpheme stress') that decides whether a following floating boundary tone H% or phrase accent H* docks onto that morpheme; the author states explicitly that this is not word stress (syllable prominence within a word) and finds no foot structure above the morpheme.

2617.prule: Main stress on the stem (root) syllable of native words (Stammsilbe = Hauptton), i.e. Germanic root stress: inseparable prefixes and derivational/inflectional Nebensilben are unstressed, so the root, normally the first syllable of a native simplex, carries the stress; nominal compounds stress the first member; unassimilated loanwords keep their source-language stress, but assimilated loans are shifted to Germanic (initial/root) stress more thoroughly than in Standard German.
2617.srule: Only in heavy compounds still felt as compounds, on the second member, and optional there (gróusmòutər ~ gróusmutər Grossmutter, bráutwùəršt Bratwurst, latǽrnə̀tsyndər Laternenanzünder); otherwise none: 'Im allgemeinen aber sind die nicht den Hauptton tragenden Silben alle gleich unbetont' (Gebhardt 1907 §18.4) -- no rhythmic secondary stress in simplex words. Concordant Schübel 1911 §27 (Stadtsteinach): Nebenton chiefly in heavy compounds with a polysyllabic or long second member, usually on a syllable separated from the Hauptton by one unstressed syllable (gróusmùdər, mýdərlà Mütterlein, Khúnəràd Konrad); Hauptton-Nebenton adjacency avoided (§24.5).

2619.dq: No stress domain is stated (no stress described). The phonological word is delimited tonally: "Another tonal word-boundary marker is a contour tone, which can only appear on the final syllable of a phonological word." 2619.tone: The 542-page grammar never uses 'stress' or 'accent' in a prosodic sense: a full-text search of the text finds only 'acute accent'/'grave accent' as tone diacritics (§II.9 'Transcription and Orthography', p.101), 'subject-prominent' (typology), the gloss 'distress' and 'stress the polarity' (question marker). The complete prosodic feature set is given as [LONG], tone and register (p.77). Tone: two levels H and L, automatic and non-automatic downstep, contour tones only word-finally (p.86), noun/verb root tone melodies with syllable-counting left-to-right association, floating L, toneless and polar-tone morphemes (§II.6), word-internal downstep and final contours as word-boundary cues (p.98), sentence tone (§II.8); 'Tone plays an extensive role, not only in distinguishing lexical items, but also in the grammar of Majang' (p.48). Independent confirmation: Getachew Anteneh Yigzaw 2014 (AAU PhD) §4.3 p.70: "Majang is a tonal language that uses pitch (high and low tone) to distinguish words in their meaning"; no stress statement anywhere in that grammar either (a full-text search: 'san "stress"' is a lexical gloss, 'accent shift' sits inside a quoted general definition of case). Joswig's SIL ms 'The Basics of Majang Tone' (7 pp.): two tone levels, contours, downstep, nothing on stress. Neither grammar denies stress explicitly; both are simply silent, so the verdict is tone or pitch accent (tone system, no stress rule), not no word stress.

2620.tone: Two contrastive tone levels H and L (Heath 2003 pp. 335, 337; Heath & Heath 1982 p. 39; Heath 1991 p. 5); HL and LH contours (LH only on long vowels; in words of more than three syllables HL only on the final syllable, 1982 p. 40); floating H and L morphotonemes, polar-tone prefixes, toneless syllables with default L, downstep and downdrift (2003 p. 337). Neither 'stress' nor 'accent' (as prominence) occurs anywhere in the 2003 chapter (a full-text search finds only 'emphasis to the noun', sec. 3.2 on noun modifiers, p. 340), in the 1982 scan, or on the 1991 pages read. The only stem-initial asymmetries are distributional (long vowels and labialized/palatalized onsets confined to the first syllable of the radical, 1982 pp. 10-11, 42-43) and are never called stress.

contra.detail: van Wijk 1890 (Spraakleer der Maleische taal, secs. 95-96 'Klemtoon', pp. 46-48) describes a very weak, durational stress on the penultimate syllable of the root word, on the final syllable only when the penult is an open syllable with pĕpĕt (schwa), kept on the root under suffixation. 2625.dq: there are no phenomena in spoken Malay corresponding to what phonologists call stress, and that the whole notion of stress is completely irrelevant in the description of Malay ... We therefore disagree with earlier researchers who have claimed stress on the penult.
2625.dloc: Sec. 10 'Conclusion' (online HTML edition of the journal, unpaginated; Internet Archive text capture)
2625.prule: No word stress. Zuraidah, Knowles & Yong 2008 (instrumental: duration and F0 of 111 words produced in citation form by two native speakers, then annotated connected speech) conclude that 'there are no phenomena in spoken Malay corresponding to what phonologists call stress'; the apparent penultimate prominence of a word said on its own is the onset rise plus final cadence of a one-word phrase, and where the penult has a central vowel (schwa) the pitch peak is delayed to the final syllable (secs. 9-10). Clynes & Deterding 2011: 265 (Standard Malay of Brunei) likewise find no inherent lexical stress: a rise-fall pitch movement across the penultimate and final syllables of a phrase 'can create an impression of penultimate word stress', and where the penult has /ə/ the movement is usually confined to the phrase-final syllable. The earlier rule (van Wijk 1890 secs. 95-96: a very weak, durational stress on the penult of the root word, on the last syllable when the penult is an open pĕpĕt (schwa) syllable, kept on the root under suffixation) is carried under the dissenting descriptions as superseded.
2625.srule: Not applicable: the descriptions followed find no word stress (Zuraidah, Knowles & Yong 2008 sec. 10: Malay 'has no stress or tone or any other intermediate level of prosodic organisation'; Clynes & Deterding 2011: 265), so no secondary stress is described. The superseded description, van Wijk 1890 sec. 96 p. 47 (quoting von de Wall), reports for literate, spelling-influenced pronunciation of suffixed words a weak 'grammatical' stress on the syllable written with the long vowel beside the root stress, 'een vaste regel bestaat er niet'; ordinary speech keeps the root stress alone.

The pitch may go up and down, loudness and tempo may increase or decrease, and on occasion the effect may be superficially similar to that produced by stress in a language like English; but these phenomena are all accounted for independently of stress. ... We therefore disagree with earlier researchers who have claim…

2626.prule: Suprasegmentals are non-phonemic; 'word stress' (tekanan kata) is decomposed into two exponents that fall on different syllables: high pitch on the OPEN INITIAL syllable (all five examples disyllabic, so initial = penult; the printed mark ['] sits after the first syllable, and the gemination remark -- the doubled consonant follows 'the stressed syllable', [ʔi-nʔ-na] -- shows the authors mean the initial syllable), and greater DURATION on the open SECOND syllable of disyllables. 2628.dq: Ang tuldik na pahilis(ˊ) ay ginagamit sa salitang Malaweg upang bigyang diin ang bigkas ng mga salita at mabigyan ng pagkakaiba ng kahulugan ng mga salitang may parehong baybay ngunit magkaiba ang kahulugan. ['... used on Malaweg words to give stress to the pronunciation of words and to distinguish the meanings of words with the same spelling ...' -- isolated citation-form words with lexical mean…
2628.dloc: Ch. 7 'Pagbabalik sa tuldik', sec. 7.1, p. 43 (Filipino version); Malaweg-language parallel 'Panoli kin daya tuldik' sec. 7.1, p. 42; sec. 1.2 'Di-titik', p. 17 (Filipino) / p. 16 (Malaweg).
2628.prule: Word stress is contrastive and lexically specified: the orthography marks it with an acute because words spelled alike differ in meaning by stress position alone; all four minimal pairs oppose penultimate vs final stress (ána/aná, bátang/batáng, bílag/bilág, pútut/putút). No default position and no distributional rule are given anywhere in the book (the book's only uses of 'diin'/'haba' for stress are secs. 1.2 and 7.1, the syllable chapter (ch. 2, 'pantig') says nothing about stress, and the Filipino stress-type terms malumay/mabilis do not occur). Sec. 1.2 equates the acute with 'stress or length', i.e. stressed vowels may be long, but this is not elaborated.
2628.srule: Not mentioned in Baloran, Manicad & Gundan 2016 (KWF Ortograpiya ng Malawég; sec. 1.2 p. 17 and ch. 7 sec. 7.1 pp. 42-43 read, full text consulted): the book says only that the acute marks stress (or length) and distinguishes homographs; no secondary or rhythmic stress is described.

2632.prule: Accent falls on the initial syllable of the lexical root ('syllabe initiale de radical', hedged 'en général'). A simple base word (root + class suffix) has one accented nucleus, the class suffix being an unaccented post-nuclear 'satellite', so in simple words the accent is word-initial; compounds and derivatives carry one accent on each root-initial syllable ('chaque première syllabe de radical porte un accent'), and the transcriptions also mark derivational prefixes ta-/ka- as accented (['ta'kana] p.189, ['ka'ce:ye] p.65). Accent is diagnosed distributionally: only accented (root-initial) syllables admit the full onset inventory ([g], [d]); intervocalic, unaccented syllables take the variants [ɣ], [r].
2632.srule: Only in complex words: a simple base word has 'un seul noyau accentué' (one accent; the class suffix is an unaccented post-nuclear satellite), whereas compounds and derivatives 'peuvent porter plus d'un seul accent par mot', one on the first syllable of each root (fushyiige ['fu'syi:ye] 'porte deux placements d'accent'; takana ['ta'kana]), each of 'le même rang qu'une syllabe initiale de mot' (equal-rank, each an 'accent primaire'). 2637.tone: Doneux 1975 (comparative noun-class study; Manjaku data from the Bok, Cur and Yu dialects) writes Manjaku with a two-way pitch contrast he calls 'ton haut' vs 'ton bas' (class prefixes ba-/bà-, ka-/kà-, p.50; 'la nasale syllabique est à ton haut' for the class-6 m- prefix in Bok, p.81) and explicitly says the same facts could be treated 'en termes d'accents' (low = unaccented). Crucially, in his summary typology of Atlantic tone (§6.2.3 'Tons', p.111) he distinguishes languages 'sans tons', 'avec tons' and a third group 'avec résidus de système tonal: manjaku, foni' — i.e. Manjaku is NOT classed as a full tone language but as one with residual tonal contrasts, which is what a pitch-accent (H-tone accent) reading amounts to. Kihm 2016 (fiche following Buis 1990's Bassarel transcription) accordingly calls the prominence 'l'accent tonique (réalisé comme un ton haut)', marked with an acute on the accented syllable (Man dé / Mán de); its placement within the 1sg subject-clitic + verb complex distinguishes completive from incompletive aspect. So the open descriptions agree on a high-pitch culminative prominence with grammatical (contrastive) placement and differ only in label (residual tone vs accent); neither gives a default position for word accent/stress. Kihm's 'Éléments de phonologie' (p.2) covers only vowels (ë, ä, e/ɛ, o/ɔ, length, weak nasalisation), d/r allophony and palatals. 2638.prule: Restricted, predictable tone; no word stress. (Virtually) every word surfaces with a high tone placed near its right edge: nominals (incl. infinitives) carry H on antepenult+penult or on the penult alone (penult-only the commoner pattern; minimal pair kilólélo 'mirror' vs kilolélo 'dry season'); verb stems are toneless and the TAM conjugation assigns H on antepenult+penult or on the penult alone (stem-initial H when an object marker is inserted in APU+PU conjugations). Tone is obligatory and demarcative but not culminative (more than one H per word), so the author rejects both 'stress language' and Hyman's word-accent for Manda.
2638.srule: Not mentioned in Bernander 2017, ch. 5 secs. 5.2.1.1 (pp. 46-47) and 5.2.4 'Tone' (pp. 54-56) read in full: the source describes no word stress and says nothing about secondary or rhythmic stress (only H-tone positions and phrase-final penult lengthening).

2638.tone: Author's own analysis (p. 54): Manda has a 'restricted' and 'predictable' tone system; 'in contrast with the claims of previous studies, Manda is not merely a stress language'; 'arguably reminiscent of an accentual system' but fails Hyman's (2014) word-accent criteria because tone is not culminative. Fn. 29 (p. 54): 'Nurse (1988) compares various languages of southern Tanzania, including Manda. He claims that Manda has lost tone altogether (together with vowel length contrast) and instead has penultimate stress (not clarifying which diagnostics of stress he uses). According to my data, none of these characterizations are satisfactory for the prosodic system of Manda.' Guthrie 1948 (grammatical tone) and Guthrie 1967-71 (no tone) also rejected there. Penult H 'often falling due to penult lenghtening' (p. 55).

tn.quote: Manda is a language with a tone system that is both “restricted” (Voorhoeve 1973; Schadeberg 1973; Marlo 2013) and “predictable” (Odden 1988). Thus, in contrast with the claims of previous studies, Manda is not merely a stress language. … all nominals in Manda (the infinitive verb included) surface with a high tone on the ante-penult and the penult … or with only a high tone on the penult … All verb stems in Manda are toneless. Instead, verb tone is assigned by the specific TAM conjugation.
